## Chapter 1

# CHAPTER XVII

PRESIDENT GRANT (1869)

The first effect of this leap into the unknown was a fit of low spirits new to the young man's education; due to the overpowering beauty of the Maryland autumn, almost unendurable for one who had toned his life down to the November grays of northern Europe. Life could not go on so beautiful and so sad. Winter came, and he was settled in bachelor's quarters far out on G Street. Congress had met; all interest centred in the new administration. The town swarmed with office-seekers, among whom a young writer was lost. He drifted among them, glad to learn his work under cover of the confusion, picking up friends on the press — all reformers jumbled in a tidal wave of expectation, waiting for General Grant to give orders.

Proverbially Washington was a poor place for education, but for young men it was paradise, since they were few and greatly in demand. After watching the abject unimportance of the young diplomat in London society, Adams found himself a young duke in Washington. He had ten years of youth to make up, and a ravenous appetite. Society went on excellently well without houses, or carriages, or jewels, or *grandezza* of any sort. Politics and reform became the detail, and waltzing the profession.

In such an atmosphere one made no great pretence of hard work, but he worked, after a fashion. He gave three months to an article on the finances of the United States and sent it to Henry Reeve, who printed it in the *Edinburgh Review*. He wanted to win a place under the vast shadow of Lord Macaulay; to a young American in 1868, such rank seemed colossal. He then set himself to a scheme for the *North American Review* — a permanent series of annual political reviews, the idea and name stolen from Lord Robert Cecil. With his sources of information at Washington, he could not help saying something that would command attention. Whether any one except his press associates ever read them, he never knew and never greatly cared.

Where he broke down was at a point where nine adventurers out of ten make their errors. One may be more or less certain of organized forces; one can never be certain of men. He belonged to the eighteenth century, and the eighteenth century upset all his plans.

Four-fifths of the American people had united in electing Grant, affected by the parallel they felt between Grant and Washington. Grant represented order. The soldier always represented order. Every one had echoed that famous phrase: "Let us have peace."

Adams could not see that this reliance on Grant was unreasonable. Newspaper-men had no great respect for the lower House; Senators had less; and Cabinet officers had none at all. One day when Adams was pleading with a Cabinet officer for patience and tact in dealing with Representatives, the Secretary impatiently broke out: "You can't use tact with a Congressman! A Congressman is a hog! You must take a stick and hit him on the snout!" Adams had but to ask: "If a Congressman is a hog, what is a Senator?" This innocent question petrified any executive officer that ever sat a week in his office.

He went to the Capitol to hear the names announced which should reveal the secret of Grant's Cabinet. To the end of his life, he wondered at the suddenness of the revolution which, within five minutes, changed his intended future into an absurdity. Grant's nominations had the singular effect of making the hearer ashamed, not so much of Grant, as of himself. He had made another total misconception of life. A great soldier might be a baby politician.

Adams left the Capitol in the same misty mental condition that had marked his railway journey to London on May 13, 1861. He knew, without absolutely saying it, that Grant had cut short the life he had laid out for himself. After such a miscarriage, no thought of effectual reform could revive for at least one generation. For the moment, he saw no hope but in following the stream.

He was taken to the White House one evening and introduced to the President. A single word with Grant satisfied him that the fewer words he risked, the better. Thus far in life he had met with but one man of the same intellectual or unintellectual type — Garibaldi. Of the two, Garibaldi seemed a trifle the more intellectual, but in both, the intellect counted for nothing; only the energy counted. The type was pre-intellectual, archaic, and would have seemed so even to the cave-dwellers. Adam, according to legend, was such a man.

In time one came to recognize the type as normal: men whose energies were the greater, the less they wasted on thought; men who sprang from the soil to power; distrustful; shy; jealous; sometimes vindictive; always needing stimulants, but for whom action was the highest stimulant — the instinct of fight. Such men were forces of nature, energies of the prime, like the *Pteraspis*, but they made short work of scholars.

Adams did not feel Grant as a hostile force; he saw only an uncertain one. Simple-minded beyond the experience of Wall Street, he resorted to commonplaces when at a loss for expression: "Let us have peace!" or, "The best way to treat a bad law is to execute it"; but sometimes he made one doubt his good faith — as when he seriously remarked to a particularly bright young woman that Venice would be a fine city if it were drained. In Mark Twain, this would have ranked among his best witticisms; in Grant it was a measure of simplicity not singular.

What worried Adams was his own education. Grant fretted and irritated him, like the *Terebratula*, as a defiance of first principles. That, two thousand years after Alexander and Cæsar, a man like Grant should be called the highest product of the most advanced evolution, made evolution ludicrous. The progress from President Washington to President Grant was alone evidence enough to upset Darwin.

Education became more perplexing at every phase. America had no use for Adams because he was eighteenth-century, and yet it worshipped Grant because he was archaic and should have lived in a cave. Yet this administration, which upset his whole life, was made up largely of friends. Secretary Fish was almost kind; Cox in the Interior promised help and comfort; Judge Hoar promised friendship.

The difficulty was not the want of friends. Grant avowed from the start a policy of drift; and a policy of drift attaches only barnacles. At thirty, one has no interest in becoming a barnacle. Grant had no objects, wanted no help, wished for no champions. The Executive asked only to be let alone. This was his meaning when he said: "Let us have peace!"

As for Adams, all his hopes of success turned on his finding an administration to support. He knew well enough the rules of self-interest. He was for sale. He wanted to be bought. His price was excessively cheap. All he wanted was something to support; something that would let itself be supported. Luck went dead against him. For once, he was fifty years in advance of his time.

## Chapter 2

# CHAPTER XVIII

FREE FIGHT (1869-1870)

Sam Hoar taught Adams the charm of Washington spring. The Potomac and its tributaries squandered beauty. Rock Creek was as wild as the Rocky Mountains. The brooding heat of the profligate vegetation; the cool charm of the running water; the terrific splendor of the June thunder-gust in the deep and solitary woods, were all sensual, animal, elemental. No European spring had shown him the same intermixture of delicate grace and passionate depravity that marked the Maryland May. He could not leave it, but loitered on into July.

In spite of the fatal undeception about Grant's political character, Adams's first winter had so much amused him that he had not a thought of change. His father knew more about Washington than any one else in Boston, and Henry was amused to find that his father's recollections of the society about President Monroe much resembled what his son felt about the society around President Johnson. He feared its effect on young men, with some justice, since it had been fatal to two of his brothers; but he understood the charm.

Henry was in a savage humor on the subject of Boston. He saw Boutwells at every counter. He found a personal grief in every tree. The climate made eternal war on society, and sex was a species of crime. Of course he was in the wrong. The thinness was in himself, not in Boston; but this is a story of education, and Adams was struggling to shape himself to his time.

Before he got back to Quincy, the effects of Grant's character showed themselves. They were startling — astounding — terrifying. The mystery that shrouded Jay Gould's classical attempt to corner gold in September, 1869, has never been cleared up. Gould was led, by the change at Washington, into the belief that he could safely corner gold without interference. To young men wasting their summer at Quincy for want of some one to hire their services at three dollars a day, such a dramatic scandal was Heaven-sent. Charles took the railway history; Henry took the so-called Gold Conspiracy; and they went to New York to work it up.

Material furnished by a government seldom satisfies critics, for it lies always under suspicion. Adams's great friends — Fish, Cox, Hoar, Evarts, Sumner — were precisely the persons most mystified. They knew less than Adams did. The Congressional Committee took a quantity of evidence which it dared not probe. The trail always faded and died out at the point where any member of the Administration became visible. Adams found out too much already, when he saw in evidence that Jay Gould had stretched his net over Grant's closest surroundings, and that Boutwell's incompetence was the bottom of Gould's calculation.

The worst scandals of the eighteenth century were relatively harmless beside this one, which smirched executive, judiciary, banks, corporate systems, professions, and people, all the great active forces of society, in one dirty cesspool of vulgar corruption. Only six months before, this innocent young man, fresh from European diplomacy, had expected to enter an honorable career in the press as the champion of a new Washington; already he foresaw a life of wasted energy.

Society is immoral and immortal; it can afford to commit any kind of folly, and indulge in any sort of vice; it cannot be killed, and the fragments that survive can always laugh at the dead; but a young man has only one chance, and brief time to seize it. At Washington, in 1869-70, every intelligent man about the Government prepared to go.

Adams could cling to Mr. Fish in the State Department, and try to make himself the recognized champion in the New York press. But when he renewed his relations with Sumner in the winter of 1869-70, he began to grasp that Sumner had a foreign policy of his own which he proposed to force on the Department. Besides the Department of State over which Fish nominally presided, there had risen a Department of Foreign Relations over which Senator Sumner ruled at the Capitol; and one made out a third Foreign Office in the War Department, with President Grant himself for chief, pressing a policy of extension in the West Indies which no Northeastern man approved.

Little by little, Sumner unfolded his foreign policy, and Adams gasped at every new article of the creed. He listened with incredulous stupor while Sumner unfolded his plan for concentrating every possible American claim against England, with a view of compelling the cession of Canada to the United States. If war was Sumner's object, and Canada were worth it, the scheme showed genius; but if he thought he could obtain Canada from England as a voluntary set-off to the Alabama Claims, he drivelled. Adams could not believe Sumner so mad as to quarrel both with Fish and with Grant. A quarrel with General Grant was lunacy.

Mr. Fish afterwards told Adams, with grim humor, that Grant took a dislike to Motley because he parted his hair in the middle. In truth, Grant disliked Motley because they had nothing in common; and for the same reason he disliked Sumner, and would dislike Adams if Adams gave him a chance.

The impending battle between Fish and Sumner was nothing like so serious as the outbreak between Hoar and Chief Justice Chase. Adams had come to Washington hoping to support the Executive in breaking down the Senate, but he never dreamed he would be required to help in breaking down the Supreme Court. He still clung to the Court, much as a churchman clings to his bishops, because they were his only symbol of unity.

Adams completed an article on the history of the Legal Tender Act for the *North American*, intending to defend the Chief Justice and the Court. The Chief Justice seemed pleased. The Attorney General, pleased or not, made no sign. The article threw Adams into opposition. Judge Hoar was implacable.

Hoar went on to demolish the Chief Justice; while Adams went on, drifting further from the Administration. Senators quarrelled with each other and with the Executive, and threw every Department into confusion. Among others they quarrelled with Hoar, and drove him from office. Adams's four most powerful friends had matched themselves, two and two, and were fighting in pairs to a finish: Sumner-Fish; Chase-Hoar; with foreign affairs and the judiciary as prizes. What value had the fight in education?

The result was a review of the Session for the July *North American* into which he crammed everything he had observed and been told. As it happened, this "Session" of 1869-70 proved his last study in current politics, and his last dying testament as a humble member of the press. The political dilemma was as clear in 1870 as it was likely to be in 1970. The system of 1789 had broken down, and with it the eighteenth-century fabric of *a priori*, or moral, principles. Politicians had tacitly given it up. Grant's administration marked the avowal. The moral law had expired — like the Constitution.

Society needed a working political system. If moral standards broke down and machinery stopped working, new morals and machinery had to be invented. Practical Americans laughed and went their way. Adams was driven to associate with Democratic Congressmen and educate them. The Administration drove him, and thousands of other young men, into active enmity to the system or want of system that had taken possession.

When spring came, he took to the woods, which were best of all. He astonished himself by remarking what a purified charm was lent to the Capitol by the greatest possible distance, as one caught glimpses of the dome over miles of forest foliage. Yet he shortened his spring, for he needed to get back to London. He had finished his New York "Gold Conspiracy," which he meant for Henry Reeve and the *Edinburgh Review*. It was the best piece of work he had done. London was a sensitive spot for the Erie management, and it was thought well to strike them where they were socially exposed. Under the excitement of chase he was becoming a pirate himself, and liked it.
